title: The Best Summer
summary: Tamra Davis discusses The Best Summer, the documentary she assembled from rediscovered footage of the Summersault festival. She reflects on filming musicians away from the stage and revisiting the backstage friendships captured on her camcorder.
transcript:
Welcome back in 1990 from the record Goo, that is Sonic Youth, of course with Kool Thing, the music video directed by the artist I'm about to play you an interview with Tamra Davis, who directed many Sonic Youth videos over the years, a legendary director and filmmaker who's had an incredibly varied career.

She did make a name for herself originally by directing music videos for Sonic Youth and The Smiths and Young MC, even Bette Midler.

Her feature film directorial credits include Adam Sandler's breakout film, Billy Madison, Britney Spears' road trip feature, Crossroads, and also her acclaimed documentary, Jean-Michel Basquiat, The Radiant Child.

Tamra's going to be heading to Australia very soon, next week in fact, from Los Angeles as a special guest of MIFF.

Her new archival documentary, The Best Summer, is screening as part of the Music on Film program that is, of course, presented by RRR.

It's a really remarkable, sort of accidental time capsule of 90s alternative music culture.

When Tamra was evacuating her Malibu home during the 2025 wildfires, as she uncovered a box of unmarked videotapes.

And what she found inside was raw, unedited footage from the 1995 Summersault Festival here in Australia.

Saying earlier, I imagine many RRR listeners would remember that iconic festival.

The lineup included acts like Beastie Boys, Sonic Youth, Beck, Bikini Kill, Pavement, Kim Deal, sort of Breeders Hiatus Project, The Amps, and what was at the time Dave Grohl's very new band, Foo Fighters as well.

At the time, Tamra was newly married to her husband, Mike D, of the Beastie Boys, and brought her camcorder along on tour, capturing an extraordinary and intimate look at these now era-defining artists at the peak of their youth in a much simpler time before smartphones and social media.

At the heart of the documentary is Riot Girl icon Kathleen Hanna from Bikini Kill, who is equipped with a microphone and conducts these really playfully kind of candid, unfiltered interviews with her fellow artists backstage.

The film also completely bypasses traditional talking head narration, and as a result, the footage really speaks for itself.

Tamra captures these really rare moments of community and creative transition with really sort of raw energy.

And I began the interview with Tamra Davis by asking her to take us back to that moment when she first discovered the footage and realised she had a whole documentary that was just sitting in a box.

Yeah, I found this box of tapes.

I have so many tapes I've been filming like kind of my whole life.

And so, you know, I was like, I should get something done with them because I was moving from a fire and I was like, oh my God, like, I should like get them digitized or something.

And so then I was like, what's on these tapes?

They just had like scribbles on them or something.

And so I had to buy a camera.

So first I bought a camera to like put them in before I just went and digitized everything because it's expensive.

And then I just saw this like beautiful little like one inch square frame.

And I was like, what?

There's like pictures.

There's like, I didn't know I shot the Foo Fighters or I didn't know I did interviews.

It was like, I just was, and I kept taking pictures of the, and even videos of the little screen off the old video camera because I just couldn't believe I had this really beautiful old footage and the quality of it.

And yeah, it had such beautiful lighting and I had no idea that I shot this whole festival.

And I had so much footage with all the interviews and everything.

It's pretty incredible.

I guess, can you take us back to 1995?

You're sort of riding high on the success of your film, Billy Madison.

You're married to Mike D from the Beastie Boys.

You've asked to jump on this tour, Summersault, which is, yeah, obviously a new festival created sort of as a rival festival to Big Day Out by Steve Pavlovic, who famously went on to found Modular Records.

Can you tell me, yeah, about your decision to head to Australia at that time?

Did you know specifically you wanted to document this tour?

No, I think it was more like Mike and I had already been together for maybe 10 years and I was like pretty well-known music video director.

And I, this was, Billy Madison was, yeah, my third movie.

And so I was kind of known as a filmmaker and I'd made videos for some of these bands.

A lot of them were my friends as well.

Mike and I got married, I think it was 93.

So it was like, we got married just like right before this.

If you have married somebody as a musician, they tour a lot.

And so if you want to see them, you kind of have to go on the road with them.

And because I was like in between making a movie, I was like, oh, this is a perfect time for me to join and go on the road with Mike.

And I love going on the road.

It's so fun.

It was so fun at that time, like just seeing them play.

And I just always had cameras with me wherever I went.

So, you know, I was like, oh, if I'm, you know, going to see them, I'm always going to film Beastie Boys stuff.

But yes, it was just more like that, that if I'm going to go on the road and be with Mike, I have so much fun hanging out.

But it just, it gives me something to do is also be filming.

It's like, it's a nice, fun hobby.

It's like I brought my paints with me or I brought a notebook to write.

You know, it's just kind of the thing that I always do.

The artists in this documentary have this really wonderful, like unguardedness to them.

We're getting to see these alternative rock icons in kind of a really unusually relaxed state.

And yeah, Kathleen Hanna's mentioned recently that back then you didn't have to carry the weight of self-consciousness because you weren't sort of constantly on camera.

How do you think, yeah, I guess like the presence of smartphones and social media today changes how artists express themselves.

And do you think you'd be able to capture the same energy in today's modern digital age?

I feel like that a lot of it is not so much the camera, but it's also the relationship with the people.

I knew all those people.

And when you're friends with people, I feel like, and also if you're a director, I feel like it's all about getting a certain kind of performance from somebody.

And so I wanted that super casual thing.

The fact that I wasn't trying to do interviews like, hi, can you meet me in your dressing room where I have a tripod and a couple of lights and, you know, I'm going to sit there next to the camera and ask you questions.

It was so like, just, I don't know.

It was a very different situation.

So I think like I could, if I knew the people, I feel like I could get like a similar thing if they were all my friends.

Everybody was also, it wasn't just they were my friends, like everybody was friends.

And I feel like that was also part of it.

Like Pav really kind of put the lineup together based on all his friends.

And so we were all people that were hanging out with each other all the time anyway.

And in the documentary, you and Kathleen Hanna sort of tag team these interviews using what you call these sort of tiger beat teeny bopper questions.

Like what's your favorite color?

What's your favorite food?

Strangely, you did get some kind of, yeah, revealing answers from these artists, from those questions.

Can you tell me about the decision to ask, I don't know, what might be considered more easier or trivial or lighthearted questions to these musicians at the time?

I think it was, I remember like Kathleen, she remembers more than I do.

I think she saw some people doing an interview, some guys, and she was like, we could do so much better than that.

And I was like, yeah, let's do it.

And I'm, I'm pretty sure what happened is like, I'm the weirdo that just like took my ticket stub.

Like it was written on my airline ticket stub, my questions.

And I was like, okay, let's write out some questions.

Like just really like kind of girly, goofy, like just playing.

And then I had my questions and then she decided to be like, I have some serious questions.

The Kathleen questions I thought were so interesting because she really wanted to know the difference between like real life and a persona.

And so her, her questions were actually quite profound and mine were like the loosen up questions.

And even so you get like a personality from, you know, the artists from that.

But I feel like her questions, she really wanted to know those things.

Looking back, it was kind of, yeah, a genius move to get Kathleen Hanna doing those interviews as well.

She's the best.

Yeah, there's some kind of fascinating conversations going on, as you mentioned, conversations about stage personas and criticism.

And yeah, what is it about like Kathleen Hanna in particular that you think makes the artists really open up in these interviews?

She's such a star.

She's so exceptional.

I mean, I love her.

I made a whole movie about her.

You know, I just think she's so fascinating.

And on that tour, a lot of people hadn't really seen them play live and seen what Bikini Kill was about.

And, you know, I kind of really tried to show everybody standing on the side of the stage because they were kind of like the baby band.

They were, you know, one of the first bands up.

Yeah.

And so I was just enamored with her.

I thought she was hilarious.

Kim Gordon and I, we were both like obsessed with her and we were trying to like match make her and Adam because we wanted her more in our lives.

So we were like, let's see if her and Adam, you know, they seem so funny together.

Like nobody would realize how great they would be together.

You know.

Yeah, it was amazing to see that that play out.

And yeah, as you mentioned, it kind of accidentally captures with this film the spark of the early romance between Kathleen Hanna and Ad-Rock, who became a couple soon after Summersault ended.

I kind of found this film a really interesting companion piece to two recent memoirs as well, like Kathleen Hanna's Rebel Girl, but also Ione Skye's memoir, Say Anything.

It was interesting, yeah, getting to read about it from both their perspectives, but also now to see this captured on film as well.

Did you feel a similar way?

Totally.

I mean, it's funny because, yeah, I really loved Ione's book.

I thought it was really wonderful and vulnerable.

And yeah, and I was like, oh, man, this is the tour that he comes back from, you know, when she's at the house.

And I was like, you know, because I was there.

I know all that stuff.

So I was like, man, that's crazy.

And then the same thing of, like, Kathleen, and she doesn't really talk that much about Adam and her book, but that was when, you know, they fell in love.

When I first did a cut, and I had this format in mind when I put it together, this day-to-day thing, you know, like day one or day two.

And I did a first version, and I had a voiceover that kind of put context to stuff.

I was like, oh, this is, you know, amazing to see Adam, so sad he's not with us.

You know, just like whatever, like I was adding little things.

And the first person I showed it to was Kim Gordon.

And Kim Gordon just was like, stop talking.

You're distracting me.

She's like, why are you adding all this voice from the future coming into the past?

And I was like, oh, my God.

And so she was like, just take it out.

Nobody needs to know any of everybody.

They'll either know where they won't or they'll Google it.

And it was a really smart thing because I feel like we're so overburdened with like, and let me give you like a billion more pieces of information.

It's like if people are interested, they'll look it up.

And otherwise, they already know when you're watching a movie.

When you know a fact and you start to see it and uncover, it was more powerful than me trying to tell you these things.

And I showed it to my kids and their generation.

They're all in their 20s and all their friends are in their 20s.

And I got a lot of feedback from them and they didn't want all the commentary.

They wanted to discover it themselves.

They didn't want it to be like, you know, somebody says a great line and then it cuts to some information that you should know, you know, whatever.

They liked that it was kind of mysterious like that and they'd have to find out if they were interested.

One of the fascinating aspects, or there's many, but another one is seeing this really raw 1995 kind of evolution of Dave Grohl, like watching it now.

It's really striking to realize that this was sort of filmed just a year after like Kurt Cobain had passed away and sort of capturing Dave in this really intensely vulnerable moment where he's really finding his feet still with Foo Fighters.

He openly admits to how much he sort of hates singing and hates talking to the audience, which feels like this kind of weird alternative reality compared to the stadium commanding Dave Grohl that we know today.

Looking back, how do you view that footage now in contrast to his sort of massive career evolution?

I know. Yeah, it's funny because he's like, yeah, what if it doesn't work out a few years later?

And, you know, and you're like, oh, my God, you're still at it.

I think it's amazing to see.

You know, I've known Dave from, you know, early days Nirvana all the way to now.

They're all still managed by the same manager.

And so we, you know, we're we see each other here and there.

And I think it's just so beautiful to see him find his voice in the film, you know, by the end of it, he's telling the crowd how much he loves them.

But getting through that time and having the support of this community, I feel like that's really present in there.

I think like I see that, but I also see I see I'm I showed it to his kids and just like seeing their reaction to it is also beautiful to me and how they never saw their dad like that.

And, you know, that to me is also interesting and also one of the reasons why I made the film is I was like, man, my kids have never really seen their dad the way I saw their dad.

And, you know, yeah, they saw, you know, the Spike movie, but that's very different in a very different context.

I was like, yeah, look at this.

This is your dad.

Yeah.

I wanted them to see that as well.

Tamra was on tour with her then husband, Mike D from the Beastie Boys and captured this incredible fly on the wall behind the scenes footage of that festival in her new archival documentary, The Best Summer, which is going to be screening very soon as part of MIFF's music on film program.

Let's jump into part two of my interview with Tamra Davis.

I guess a lot of music festival culture from the early 90s really had that sort of hyper masculine energy to it as well.

And with the lineups too.

But yeah, your lens gives us this really beautiful, almost like feminist sort of subtext to the film.

Like you're behind the camera.

Kathleen's doing the interviews.

There's Kim Gordon navigating the realities of motherhood and life on the road.

When you first dug up those tapes, did you, yeah, sort of immediately recognize how kind of radical it was to have that documented in that era?

It was actually something I was looking for because it just, it had happened recently that I showed a short film I made.

I made a feature on Jean-Michel Basquiat, but I have a short that's just the footage of him and I talking and me being in the studio with him.

And afterwards, all these women came up to me talking about how they saw how he talked to me and how the female gaze really affected his performance and how he spoke and his honesty and vulnerability and how powerful that was.

So to me, I was like, wow, this is really interesting.

When I looked at my film, I was like, you can really see that the female gaze and the way everybody talks to me and Catholic that it, it's like, it's different and it's powerful.

And it's like, that's the thing as a young girl filming when I started out.

And even to now it's like, it's so hard to be a female filmmaker.

The stats are even worse than they were before.

And so I'm trying to show that it's like, yeah, we're different, but it's like, look at the strengths of this.

And that was the thing I really wanted to show is like, yeah, it's difficult to be a female filmmaker, but when you give us a camera and you give us an opportunity, look at the strengths that we also have.

Like that's also part of it.

It's not just like, oh, there's no difference.

It's just, it's like, yeah, sometimes there is a difference and it's actually really fucking amazing.

You know, it's good.

And that a whole girl shot an entire movie.

You know, I just look at that and I'm like, yeah, like this whole movie shot just by one girl.

And you know, I want girls to be inspired by that.

And I think that there is something.

Yeah.

About the female gaze and what my eye goes to on the stage.

And you know, the, the flirty, you know, kind of that I have with people that are just whatever.

It's more like fun.

It's not like dude upon dude.

I like leaning into that.

I think there's something really strong about that.

And I hope it inspires people, not just girls, but also people that are different.

Knowing that you're who you are as an individual is authentic and it affects the tone of your film.

Kathleen Hanna's described you as someone that just makes things happen.

Is that sort of fearless quality something that resonates with you about yourself?

I think so.

I mean, I feel like you can't do the things I've done without making things happen.

Like you have to just be like, okay, I'm going to make a film or okay, I'm going to shoot this or okay.

Like you just, you have to be super ambitious like that.

I am pretty fearless in that way.

But I think like, that's what, that's what I liked about Kathleen and I, even though we're very different people and come from different places that we both have that energy that it's like, yeah, let's start a band.

Let's make a movie.

Let's shoot a documentary.

I'm like, okay.

Yeah.

She didn't become who she was because she didn't have that energy as well.

And I think like when you find another friend like that and a, at a summer camp, I think like that energy is just really special.

And when you find that in another person, guy, girl, whoever, that's what gets things done.

That's how you start bands, how you make movies, how you create a scene.

You've captured some really incredible onstage performances as well.

There's, yeah, scenes of Sonic Youth on stage with those strobe lights almost covering the band members in these sort of flashes of lightning.

And there's Dave Grohl running out to stage with the Beastie Boys screaming on sabotage.

When you sent the film to these bands to prove, what was their reaction?

Did they sort of appreciate those moments being so lovingly preserved in that way?

Yeah.

I feel like they loved it just as much as me because first of all, there's nothing like seeing yourself from 30 years ago and you're gorgeous.

You know, like everybody looks good 30 years ago.

Like we're all like babies, but so cute.

And the fashion is so good.

And, and I shoot, I am such a fan.

Like I'm one of their biggest fans.

So like I shoot it with the love of a fan.

My eye is if I was in the front row shooting it and I'm shooting like my favorite people and what I want to look at.

So yeah, when you see Sonic Youth, like I pretty much have the camera on Kim Gordon most of the time.

Like I just think she's so amazing to look at always.

And you know, yes, Al Thurston's incredible as well, but I'm always like, oh my God, Kim, how does she do it with those shoes?

You know, panning down to her feet.

So I feel like everyone really loved it.

And in the end, I think Kim was really right.

I think everybody liked that.

I didn't add anything in because there wasn't anything controversial about it.

It was like, this is who everybody was, what everybody said and what the music was like.

Everybody approved it.

That process went very well.

And if anybody had a note, Mike, that was my favorite thing is I felt like I was happy to do a note, whatever it could possibly be, even just because it felt more like a collaboration or, and I just, whatever, I've been working on projects where you get notes always from like your executives and those are different kinds of notes.

So it felt really, I liked showing it to them, knowing that if anybody had anything or any comments, it was so easy to do.

And I loved it.

Yeah.

You mentioned Dave Grohl's kids seeing the film.

I understand for the early screenings of the film, also like Kim Gordon and Steve Malkmus were in the audience sitting next to their daughters as well who are featured as, yeah, as babies in the documentary.

Can you tell me more about how it felt to watch the film on the big screen?

And these must've been special moments for those artists too, to share with their kids.

Yeah.

Like it was one of the most incredible experiences.

And I think also for Coco to see her life framed like that, like how loving her parents were and how her mom, like, it's just was a beautiful way to like see your life.

And, you know, it was just, I think it really, it really helped her.

Like it was, I mean, like, it was like such a wonderful way to see your childhood.

Like every, like everyone loved you.

And yeah.

And I think also at Lottie, Steven's daughter, she came and spent a summer with us.

She was like one of the first persons I showed it to as well.

So for her to see her dad at that time.

And that, you know, it was, I don't know, it was really important to me.

Yeah.

And Lose, who's Yalke's daughter.

To me, it's just, you know, I, I, I know all these kids now and they're the next generation.

They're all making music and doing cool, creative things.

And I mean, for my boys, this was one of my, their favorite films that I've done.

I'm like, really?

This is your favorite?

Yeah.

And they're like, yeah, by far, this is our favorite phone.

I was like, thanks.

I guess that's a compliment.

You know.

You screened it in Sydney.

You're about to screen it in Melbourne.

How does it feel getting to show this film on the big screen?

Especially to like Australian audiences who were perhaps there for Summersault in 1995.

Yeah.

There was a moment that I asked the audience who was there and like half the audience raised their hand.

It made me so excited because they were there as well.

And, and I feel like it's a shared experience.

It's one of the strange things that happens on the film.

It's all point of view.

So you hear my voice, but I'm not really a presence.

I really tried to make it feel like it's your experience.

I didn't want it to be about me.

I wanted it to be about like a person's point of view.

So, um, I'm hoping that the people had that similar experience or to me, it's almost like the fantasy version of the perfect experience.

Cause now you've got to go backstage with all those people that you saw.

We don't have a film like this for that time.

You know, there's Woodstock 99, but that's like a horror film as far as I'm concerned.

I was like, I was trying to make the opposite of that.

So I was just like, yeah, that, that these bands are so important for our culture.

And you know, we're, yeah, the evolution of music.

And I'm just so happy that I had this footage and it's, I'm so grateful.

And sometimes, yeah.

Also the, sometimes it takes 30 years before you, you know, if I made it then, I don't know if it would have been the film it is now.

So I think there's something really cool about art that sometimes a painting, a piece of art, sometimes things take a little while before it finds itself.

Thank you very much for this film and for the chat today.

Of course, you're a guest of MIFF for the festival.

Thank you.
